in_hebrew.name: יוני
in_hebrew.long_meaning: יוני היא חודש קיץ, חודש הקיץ, והיא נקראת על שם כוכב היונה, אשר נראה בשמיים. באופן רוחני, יוני יכולה לסמל רננות, חיים ואופטימיות. במסורת הנוצרית, יוני עשויה לסמל את החיים האידאליים, כאשר הכוכבים נראים בתהלוכה בשמיים.

in_greek.name: Ιούνης
in_greek.meaning: μήνας του καλοκαιριού, μήνας της θερμότητας
in_greek.long_meaning: Ο Ιούνης είναι ο μήνας του καλοκαιριού, ο μήνας της θερμότητας και της ξηρασίας. Στη ρωμανική γλώσσα, ο Ιούνης ήταν ο μήνας του έρωτα και της αγάπης. Στη Χριστιανική παράδοση, ο Ιούνης είναι συνδεδεμένος με την εορτή της Αγίας Ελένης, η οποία γιορτάζεται την 1η Ιουνίου.

in_latin.name: Iunius
in_latin.long_meaning: Iunius est mensis aestivus, mensis caloris et siccitatis. In traditione Romana, Iunius erat mensis amoris et caritatis. In Ecclesia Christiana, Iunius est connectus cum festo Sanctae Helenae, quae celebratur die 1 Iunii.

biblical_reference.note: The name June is not directly mentioned in the Bible, but it is associated with the month of June, which was named after the Roman goddess Juno.

historical_references.reference: The Roman goddess Juno was the wife and sister of Jupiter. She was regarded as the queen of the gods in the Roman pantheon and was the goddess of marriage, childbirth, and the protector of the Roman state.
historical_references.context: Juno was the name of the Roman goddess, and the Christian month of June may have been named in her honor.

historical_references.reference: The Roman calendar, which was used in the Roman Empire, had ten months and began with March. Numa Pompilius, the second king of Rome, is traditionally credited with adding two months, January and February, to the Roman calendar around 700 BC. Later, Julius Caesar added two months, July and Augustus, to the Roman calendar in 46 BC and 8 BC, respectively.
historical_references.time_period: Roman Republic (8th century BC - 27 BC) / Roman Empire (44 BC - 4th century AD)
historical_references.context: The early Roman calendar did not include a month corresponding to our modern June. It is believed that when the Roman calendar was reorganized, the months of May and Quintilis (Latin for 'fifth month') were renamed in honor of the Roman deities Maia and Jupiter, respectively, resulting in the modern names of May and June.
